title: Medical Terminology
summary: Medical words are built from a small set of parts, so you decode instead of memorize. This module gives you the parts, the directions, the map of the body, and the abbreviations you will actually hear.

lessons.title: How medical words are built
lessons.body:
## Built, not memorized

Most medical vocabulary is assembled from a small inventory of parts. Learn roughly `100` parts and you can decode thousands of words you have never seen before.

Every term has up to three pieces.

- **Root** — the body part or the core idea. `cardi` is heart, `nephr` is kidney.
- **Prefix** — sits in front and usually changes amount, speed, position, or turns the meaning negative. `brady-` is slow, `hyper-` is above normal.
- **Suffix** — sits on the end and usually says what is happening: a condition, a symptom, or a procedure. `-itis` is inflammation, `-ectomy` is surgical removal.

Not every word uses all three. `Gastritis` is root plus suffix. `Tachycardia` is prefix plus root plus suffix.

## The combining vowel

Roots are usually written with a slash and a vowel, as in `cardi/o` or `nephr/o`. That `o` is a **combining vowel** and it exists only to make the word pronounceable.

The rule has two halves.

1. Keep the vowel when the next part begins with a **consonant**. `cardi` plus `megaly` gives `cardiomegaly`.
2. Drop the vowel when the next part begins with a **vowel**. `cardi` plus `itis` gives `carditis`, not `cardioitis`.

Between two roots, keep the vowel no matter what. `gastr/o` plus `enter/o` plus `-itis` gives `gastroenteritis`, inflammation of stomach and small intestine.

> **Key:** The combining vowel carries no meaning at all. When you decode a word, ignore it completely.

## The decoding method

Read a medical word **backwards**: suffix first, then prefix, then root.

Take `pericarditis`.

1. `-itis` means inflammation
2. `peri-` means around
3. `cardi` means heart

Inflammation of the tissue around the heart. Correct.

Take `hypoglycemia`.

1. `-emia` means blood condition
2. `hypo-` means below normal
3. `glyc` means sugar

Below-normal sugar in the blood. Correct again.

Take `intramuscular`.

1. `-ar` means pertaining to
2. `intra-` means within
3. `muscul` means muscle

Pertaining to within the muscle, which is exactly what an `IM` injection is.

> **On the exam:** You will meet terms nobody taught you. Decode from the back and you will get most of them right without having memorized any of them.

## Two cautions

**Near-twin roots.** `Ren/o` and `nephr/o` both mean kidney, one from Latin and one from Greek, and both are correct. But `my/o` means muscle while `myel/o` means spinal cord or bone marrow, and mixing those two changes the diagnosis completely.

**Plurals are irregular**, because the source languages are Latin and Greek.

| Singular | Plural |
|---|---|
| diagnosis | diagnoses |
| bacterium | bacteria |
| vertebra | vertebrae |
| bronchus | bronchi |
| thorax | thoraces |
| apex | apices |

> **Trap:** `Hyper-` and `hypo-` differ by two letters and mean opposite things. Read fast or written sloppily, they are the most dangerous near-twins in the language. Read the whole word every time.
keyPoints: Every medical term is some combination of root, prefix and suffix.
The combining vowel (usually o) exists for pronunciation and carries no meaning.
Keep the combining vowel before a consonant, drop it before a vowel, keep it between two roots.
Decode backwards: suffix, then prefix, then root.
Hyper- and hypo- are opposites two letters apart; my/o and myel/o are unrelated.

checks.q: Using the combining vowel rule, which spelling is correct?
choices: Gastroenteritis means inflammation of the stomach only
checks.why: The suffix -itis begins with a vowel, so the combining vowel is dropped and gastr plus itis becomes gastritis. Gastroenteritis is a real word but it means stomach and small intestine together.

checks.q: Decode pericarditis using the backwards method.
choices: Inflammation of the tissue around the heart
checks.why: The suffix -itis is inflammation, the prefix peri- is around, and the root cardi is heart. Removal would be -ectomy, inside would be endo-, and enlargement would be -megaly.

checks.q: Which pair of roots means the same thing?
checks.why: Nephr/o is Greek for kidney and ren/o is Latin for kidney, so both are correct and both appear in practice. My/o is muscle while myel/o is spinal cord or bone marrow, which is the dangerous near-twin to avoid.

lessons.title: Core roots, part one: organs and systems
lessons.body:
## The root is the subject of the sentence

The root names the body part the word is about. Everything else describes it. These twelve roots carry most of what you will hear in a shift.

| Root | Meaning | Built example |
|---|---|---|
| `cardi/o` | heart | `cardiomyopathy`, disease of heart muscle |
| `pulmon/o` | lung | `cardiopulmonary`, heart and lungs together |
| `pneum/o`, `pneumon/o` | lung, or air | `pneumothorax`, air in the chest cavity |
| `hepat/o` | liver | `hepatitis`, inflammation of the liver |
| `nephr/o` | kidney (Greek) | `nephrectomy`, surgical removal of a kidney |
| `ren/o` | kidney (Latin) | `renal failure`, kidney failure |
| `neur/o` | nerve | `neuropathy`, nerve disease |
| `oste/o` | bone | `osteomyelitis`, infection of bone and marrow |
| `derm/o`, `dermat/o` | skin | `dermatitis`, inflamed skin |
| `gastr/o` | stomach | `gastrectomy`, removal of the stomach |
| `enter/o` | small intestine | `enteritis`, inflamed small intestine |
| `col/o`, `colon/o` | large intestine, colon | `colonoscopy`, looking inside the colon |

## Why two roots for one kidney

Medicine inherited vocabulary from both Greek and Latin, and both survived. As a working rule, the Greek root tends to show up in disease and procedure names while the Latin root shows up as an adjective.

You will see `nephrology`, `nephrectomy` and `nephritis` on one side, and `renal failure`, `renal artery` and `renal function` on the other. Same organ, two vocabularies.

The same doubling happens elsewhere: `pulmon/o` is Latin for lung and `pneumon/o` is Greek. `Pulmonary embolism` and `pneumonia` refer to the same organ.

> **Key:** When two roots mean the same organ, you are not learning two facts. You are learning one organ with two accents.

## Stacking roots

Roots combine freely, which is how long words get built.

- `gastr/o` + `enter/o` + `-logy` gives `gastroenterology`, the study of stomach and intestine
- `cardi/o` + `my/o` + `-pathy` gives `cardiomyopathy`, disease of heart muscle
- `oste/o` + `myel/o` + `-itis` gives `osteomyelitis`, inflammation of bone and marrow
- `neur/o` + `-logy` gives `neurology`, while `neur/o` + `-pathy` gives `neuropathy`

Decoding still runs backwards. Find the suffix, then work leftward through the roots.

## The traps inside this set

`Pneum/o` means both lung and air, and context decides which. A `pneumothorax` is air in the chest, not a lung in the chest. `Pneumonia` is infection in the lung tissue itself.

`Hepat/o` and `hemat/o` look similar in handwriting and mean completely different things: liver versus blood. A `hepatoma` is a liver tumor; a `hematoma` is a collected pocket of blood.

`Enter/o` is specifically small intestine, while `col/o` is large intestine. `Gastroenteritis` is the stomach-and-small-bowel illness that produces vomiting and diarrhea; `colitis` is a different problem in a different place.

> **Trap:** `Osteomyelitis` contains `myel/o`, which here means bone marrow, not spinal cord. The same root serves both meanings and the neighboring root tells you which.

> **On shift:** When a chart says a patient has `ESRD` on `HD`, you are reading end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis. Both kidney words are in play at once, and both point at the same failing organ.
keyPoints: Cardi/o heart, pulmon/o and pneum/o lung, hepat/o liver, nephr/o and ren/o kidney, neur/o nerve.
Oste/o bone, derm/o skin, gastr/o stomach, enter/o small intestine, col/o large intestine.
Greek roots usually build disease and procedure names; Latin roots usually build adjectives.
Roots stack freely, and decoding still runs backwards from the suffix.
Hepat/o (liver) and hemat/o (blood) are visually similar and clinically unrelated.

checks.q: What does osteomyelitis mean?
choices: Inflammation of bone and bone marrow
Inflammation of the spinal cord only
checks.why: Oste/o is bone, myel/o is marrow or spinal cord, and -itis is inflammation. The neighboring root oste/o tells you marrow is the intended meaning here rather than spinal cord.

checks.q: A patient has a pneumothorax. What is in the chest cavity?
checks.why: Pneum/o carries two meanings, lung and air, and in pneumothorax it means air. Blood in the chest would be hemothorax, and infection in lung tissue is pneumonia.

checks.q: Which term refers to disease of the heart muscle?
checks.why: Cardi/o is heart, my/o is muscle, and -pathy is disease, so cardiomyopathy is disease of the heart muscle. Cardiomegaly is enlargement, pericarditis is inflammation around the heart, and cardiology is the study of the heart.

lessons.title: Core roots, part two: blood, vessels, airway and the rest
lessons.body:
## Blood, vessels and muscle

| Root | Meaning | Built example |
|---|---|---|
| `hem/o`, `hemat/o` | blood | `hemothorax`, blood in the chest cavity |
| `angi/o` | vessel (any) | `angiography`, imaging of vessels |
| `vas/o` | vessel, duct | `vasoconstriction`, narrowing of vessels |
| `phleb/o` | vein | `phlebotomy`, cutting into a vein to draw blood |
| `arteri/o` | artery | `arteriosclerosis`, hardening of arteries |
| `my/o` | muscle | `myalgia`, muscle pain |
| `arthr/o` | joint | `arthroscopy`, looking inside a joint |
| `cyt/o` | cell | `cytology`, the study of cells |

`Angi/o` and `vas/o` both mean vessel. `Angi/o` shows up in imaging and procedures, as in `angioplasty`. `Vas/o` shows up in physiology words, as in `vasodilation` and `vasopressor`.

## Head and nervous system

| Root | Meaning | Built example |
|---|---|---|
| `cephal/o` | head | `cephalalgia`, headache |
| `encephal/o` | brain | `encephalitis`, inflammation of the brain |
| `mening/o` | membranes covering the brain and cord | `meningitis` |
| `myel/o` | spinal cord, or bone marrow | `myelopathy` |

Notice `encephal/o` is literally `en-` (inside) plus `cephal/o` (head). The brain is the thing inside the head, which is exactly what the word says.

> **Key:** When a root looks long, check whether it is actually a prefix glued onto a shorter root. `Encephal/o` and `endocardi/o` both decode that way.

## Airway and chest

| Root | Meaning | Built example |
|---|---|---|
| `rhin/o` | nose | `rhinorrhea`, runny nose |
| `laryng/o` | voice box | `laryngospasm`, spasm of the voice box |
| `trache/o` | windpipe | `tracheostomy`, surgical opening into the trachea |
| `bronch/o` | large airway branches | `bronchodilator`, a drug that widens bronchi |
| `thorac/o` | chest | `thoracotomy`, surgical opening of the chest |
| `abdomin/o` | abdomen | `abdominal` |

## Bladder, sugar, stone, disease

| Root | Meaning | Built example |
|---|---|---|
| `cyst/o` | bladder, or fluid-filled sac | `cystitis`, bladder infection |
| `glyc/o`, `gluc/o` | sugar, glucose | `hyperglycemia`, high blood sugar |
| `lith/o` | stone | `nephrolithiasis`, kidney stones |
| `path/o` | disease | `pathology`, the study of disease |
| `py/o` | pus | `pyuria`, pus in the urine |
| `ot/o` | ear | `otitis media`, middle ear infection |
| `ophthalm/o` | eye | `ophthalmology` |
| `hyster/o` | uterus | `hysterectomy` |

## Putting it to work

Decode `cholecystitis`: `-itis` is inflammation, `chol/e` is bile, `cyst` is the sac. Inflammation of the gallbladder, the sac that holds bile.

Decode `cholelithiasis`: `-iasis` is a condition, `lith` is stone, `chol/e` is bile. Gallstones.

Decode `encephalopathy`: `-pathy` is disease, `encephal/o` is brain. Brain disease, a deliberately vague word for a brain that is not working right.

Decode `thrombophlebitis`: `-itis` is inflammation, `phleb/o` is vein, `thromb/o` is clot. An inflamed vein with a clot in it.

> **Trap:** `Cyst/o` means bladder in `cystitis` but means any fluid-filled sac in `cholecystitis`. The neighboring root decides, which is why you never translate a root in isolation.

> **On shift:** `Hem/o` shows up everywhere and each version is a different problem: `hemothorax` is blood in the chest, `hematoma` is a pocket of blood in tissue, `hematuria` is blood in the urine, `hemoptysis` is coughing up blood, and `hematemesis` is vomiting blood.
keyPoints: Hem/o and hemat/o blood, angi/o and vas/o vessel, phleb/o vein, arteri/o artery.
Cephal/o head, encephal/o brain, myel/o cord or marrow, mening/o the coverings.
Rhin/o nose, laryng/o voice box, trache/o windpipe, bronch/o airway branches, thorac/o chest.
Cyst/o bladder or sac, glyc/o sugar, lith/o stone, path/o disease, py/o pus.
Roots change meaning with their neighbors, so never translate one in isolation.

checks.q: What is a hemothorax?
choices: A clot in a leg vein
checks.why: Hem/o is blood and thorac/o is chest, so a hemothorax is blood collecting in the chest cavity. Air in the chest is a pneumothorax and a clot in a leg vein is a deep vein thrombosis.

checks.q: Decode nephrolithiasis.
checks.why: Nephr/o is kidney, lith is stone, and -iasis means a condition, giving kidney stones. Inflammation would be nephritis, removal would be nephrectomy, and blood in urine is hematuria.

checks.q: A patient is described as having hemoptysis. What are they doing?
checks.why: Hem/o is blood and -ptysis means spitting, so hemoptysis is blood coughed up from the airway. Vomiting blood is hematemesis and blood in urine is hematuria, which are different sources and different problems.

lessons.title: Prefixes: amount, speed, position, negation
lessons.body:
## Prefixes modify, they do not name

A prefix never tells you which body part is involved. It tells you how much, how fast, where, or whether the thing is present at all.

## Amount and degree

| Prefix | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `hyper-` | above normal, excessive | `hyperglycemia`, high blood sugar |
| `hypo-` | below normal, deficient | `hypotension`, low blood pressure |
| `poly-` | many, much | `polyuria`, excessive urination |
| `olig-`, `oligo-` | few, scanty | `oliguria`, scanty urine output |
| `an-`, `a-` | without, absence of | `apnea`, no breathing |
| `dys-` | difficult, painful, abnormal | `dyspnea`, difficult breathing |
| `eu-` | normal, good | `eupnea`, normal breathing |

`Hyper-` and `hypo-` are the pair that matters most and the pair most easily confused. `Hypertension` is high blood pressure and `hypotension` is low, and they call for opposite responses.

## Speed

`Tachy-` means fast and `brady-` means slow. Attach either to a root and you get a vital sign abnormality.

- `tachycardia`, fast heart rate, in an adult over `100` beats per minute
- `bradycardia`, slow heart rate, in an adult under `60` beats per minute
- `tachypnea`, fast breathing, in an adult over `20` breaths per minute
- `bradypnea`, slow breathing, in an adult under `12` breaths per minute

> **Key:** `Tachy-` plus `cardi/o` plus `-ia` is not a word to memorize. It is three parts you already know, assembled.

## Position and relationship

| Prefix | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `peri-` | around | `pericardium`, sac around the heart |
| `epi-` | upon, above | `epidermis`, outer layer of skin |
| `endo-` | within, inner | `endotracheal`, inside the trachea |
| `sub-` | under, below | `sublingual`, under the tongue |
| `supra-` | above | `suprapubic`, above the pubic bone |
| `intra-` | within | `intramuscular`, within the muscle |
| `inter-` | between | `intercostal`, between the ribs |
| `trans-` | across, through | `transdermal`, through the skin |
| `retro-` | behind | `retrosternal`, behind the sternum |

`Intra-` and `inter-` differ by one letter and mean different things. `Intramuscular` puts the needle in the muscle; `intercostal` muscles sit between the ribs.

## Time and sequence

`Pre-` means before, `post-` means after. `Preoperative` is before surgery, `postictal` is the confused period after a seizure.

## Number and side

| Prefix | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `hemi-` | half | `hemiparesis`, weakness on one side |
| `bi-` | two | `bilateral`, both sides |
| `uni-` | one | `unilateral`, one side |
| `quadri-` | four | `quadriplegia`, paralysis of all four limbs |
| `para-` | beside, or two like parts | `paraplegia`, paralysis of both legs |

## Against

`Anti-` and `contra-` both mean against. `Antiemetic` opposes vomiting, `antipyretic` opposes fever, and a `contraindication` is a reason a treatment should not be given.

> **Trap:** `Hemi-` and `semi-` both suggest half, but `hemi-` is anatomic (`hemiparesis` is one side of the body) while `semi-` is descriptive (`semi-Fowler's` is a partly raised position). They are not interchangeable.

> **On the exam:** Questions love `dysphagia` versus `dysphasia`. `Phag/o` is swallowing and `phas/o` is speech, so one is trouble swallowing and the other is trouble speaking. Both appear in stroke stems.
keyPoints: Hyper- is above normal and hypo- is below normal; they are opposites two letters apart.
Tachy- is fast and brady- is slow: adult tachycardia over 100, bradycardia under 60, tachypnea over 20.
Position prefixes: peri- around, epi- upon, endo- within, sub- under, intra- within, inter- between.
Hemi- half, bi- two, uni- one, quadri- four, para- beside or two like parts.
A-/an- is absence, dys- is difficult or abnormal, eu- is normal.

checks.q: An adult with a respiratory rate of 26 has which finding?
checks.why: Tachy- is fast and -pnea is breathing, and adult tachypnea means a rate over 20 per minute. Bradypnea would be under 12, apnea is no breathing at all, and eupnea is a normal rate.

checks.q: What does quadriplegia describe?
choices: Weakness on one side of the body
Loss of sensation in the hands
checks.why: Quadri- is four and -plegia is paralysis. Weakness on one side is hemiparesis, and paralysis of both legs is paraplegia, which is para- plus -plegia.

checks.q: A stroke patient cannot get words out but swallows normally. Which term fits?
checks.why: Phas/o refers to speech, so dysphasia is difficulty speaking. Dysphagia uses phag/o for swallowing, dyspnea is difficult breathing, and dysuria is painful urination.

lessons.title: Suffixes: conditions, symptoms and procedures
lessons.body:
## The suffix tells you what kind of word it is

Decode backwards because the suffix sets the category. Once you know whether you are reading a disease, a symptom, or an operation, the rest falls into place.

## Conditions and diseases

| Suffix | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `-itis` | inflammation | `appendicitis` |
| `-osis` | abnormal condition | `cyanosis`, a blue condition |
| `-emia` | blood condition | `anemia`, lacking blood cells |
| `-uria` | urine condition | `hematuria`, blood in urine |
| `-pathy` | disease | `neuropathy`, nerve disease |
| `-oma` | tumor, mass | `hematoma`, a mass of blood |
| `-megaly` | enlargement | `cardiomegaly`, enlarged heart |
| `-sclerosis` | hardening | `atherosclerosis` |
| `-iasis` | presence of, condition | `cholelithiasis`, gallstones |

## Symptoms

| Suffix | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `-algia`, `-dynia` | pain | `myalgia`, muscle pain |
| `-pnea` | breathing | `dyspnea`, difficult breathing |
| `-rrhage`, `-rrhagia` | bursting forth, heavy bleeding | `hemorrhage` |
| `-rrhea` | flow, discharge | `rhinorrhea`, runny nose |
| `-plegia` | paralysis | `hemiplegia` |
| `-paresis` | weakness, partial paralysis | `hemiparesis` |
| `-emesis` | vomiting | `hematemesis`, vomiting blood |
| `-phagia` | swallowing, eating | `dysphagia` |
| `-esthesia` | sensation | `paresthesia`, abnormal tingling |

`-Plegia` and `-paresis` are a pair worth separating. Paralysis means no movement at all. Paresis means weakness with some movement preserved, and that distinction changes how a stroke is described and scored.

> **Key:** One `r` or two changes the word. `-rrhea` is a flow (runny nose, diarrhea), `-rrhage` is a burst (hemorrhage). Same idea, different violence.

## Procedures

| Suffix | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `-ectomy` | surgical removal | `appendectomy` |
| `-otomy` | cutting into | `thoracotomy` |
| `-ostomy` | creating a permanent opening | `colostomy` |
| `-plasty` | surgical repair or reshaping | `angioplasty` |
| `-scopy` | looking inside with an instrument | `colonoscopy` |
| `-gram` | the record or image produced | `electrocardiogram` |
| `-graphy` | the process of recording | `angiography` |
| `-centesis` | puncture to withdraw fluid | `thoracentesis` |
| `-pexy` | surgical fixation | `nephropexy` |

The three that get confused are `-otomy`, `-ostomy` and `-ectomy`. A `tracheotomy` cuts into the trachea. A `tracheostomy` leaves a permanent opening there. A `nephrectomy` takes the kidney out entirely.

## Study and specialist

`-logy` is the study of something and `-logist` is the person who studies it. `Cardiology` is the field, `cardiologist` is the physician, and the same pattern runs through `neurology`, `nephrology` and `pathology`.

## Assembling and taking apart

Decode `bronchoscopy`: looking inside the bronchi. Decode `splenomegaly`: enlarged spleen. Decode `dysrhythmia`: `dys-` abnormal, `rhythm`, `-ia` condition, so an abnormal heart rhythm. Decode `paresthesia`: `para-` abnormal or beside, `-esthesia` sensation, so the pins-and-needles feeling.

> **Trap:** `-Emia` refers to the blood, not to bleeding. `Bacteremia` is bacteria in the blood, `hypoxemia` is low oxygen in the blood, and `uremia` is urea waste in the blood. None of them means hemorrhage.

> **On shift:** An `ECG` and an `EKG` are the same test, one spelled from English and one from the German `Elektrokardiogramm`. The `-gram` at the end tells you both words name the printed record.
keyPoints: -itis inflammation, -osis abnormal condition, -emia blood condition, -uria urine condition, -oma mass, -megaly enlargement.
-algia pain, -pnea breathing, -rrhea flow, -rrhage burst of bleeding, -plegia paralysis, -paresis weakness.
-ectomy removal, -otomy cutting into, -ostomy permanent opening, -plasty repair, -scopy looking, -gram the image.
-logy is the field and -logist is the specialist.
-emia always means a blood condition, never bleeding.

checks.q: What is the difference between a tracheotomy and a tracheostomy?
choices: A tracheotomy removes the trachea; a tracheostomy repairs it
A tracheotomy cuts into the trachea; a tracheostomy creates a permanent opening
They are identical procedures with two spellings
A tracheostomy is diagnostic; a tracheotomy is therapeutic
checks.why: -otomy means cutting into and -ostomy means creating a permanent opening, which is the difference between a temporary incision and a stoma you can see on the neck. Removal would require -ectomy.

checks.q: A stroke patient can move the right arm weakly but not normally. Which suffix applies?
choices: -plegia, because any movement deficit is paralysis
-paresis, because weakness with preserved movement is not paralysis
checks.why: Paresis is weakness with some movement retained, while plegia is complete paralysis with no movement. Describing partial weakness as plegia overstates the deficit and changes how the case is triaged.

checks.q: Which term names a blood condition rather than an act of bleeding?
checks.why: The suffix -emia denotes a condition of the blood, so bacteremia is bacteria present in the blood. Hemorrhage and menorrhagia both use -rrhage for bursting forth, and rhinorrhea is a flow from the nose.

lessons.title: Directions and positions
lessons.body:
## Everything is described from anatomical position

Directional terms only work if everyone agrees on a starting posture. That posture is **anatomical position**: standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward.

Directions are always described from the patient's perspective, not yours. The patient's left is on your right when you face them, and getting that backwards puts an injury on the wrong side of the chart.

> **Key:** Left and right always belong to the patient. Say it out loud when you document.

## The core pairs

| Term | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Superior / inferior | above / below | The heart is superior to the stomach |
| Anterior (ventral) / posterior (dorsal) | front / back | The sternum is anterior to the spine |
| Medial / lateral | toward midline / away from midline | The thumb is lateral to the pinky |
| Proximal / distal | closer to / farther from the trunk | The elbow is proximal to the wrist |
| Superficial / deep | nearer the surface / farther in | Skin is superficial to muscle |
| Bilateral / unilateral | both sides / one side | Bilateral breath sounds |

`Proximal` and `distal` apply mainly to limbs and always reference the point of attachment to the trunk. A wrist injury is distal to the elbow, and a pulse felt below an injury is called a distal pulse, which is how you check whether a splint cut off circulation.

`Ventral` and `dorsal` are the older animal terms. In humans, ventral equals anterior and dorsal equals posterior, which is why the top of the foot is the dorsum and a `dorsalis pedis` pulse is felt there.

## Body positions you will place patients in

| Position | What it is | When used |
|---|---|---|
| Supine | flat on the back, face up | Default for assessment and CPR |
| Prone | flat on the stomach, face down | Some back exams, certain ventilated patients |
| Lateral recumbent | lying on one side | Left lateral is the standard side |
| Recovery position | on the side, head supported, top knee forward | Unresponsive patient who is breathing and has a pulse |
| Fowler's | sitting upright, about `60`–`90` degrees | Breathing difficulty |
| Semi-Fowler's | head raised about `30`–`45` degrees | Comfort, reflux, mild respiratory distress |
| Trendelenburg | flat with the feet elevated, whole body tilted head-down | Historically used for shock, now rarely recommended |
| Shock position | supine with legs raised `6`–`12` inches | Varies by protocol; many services have dropped it |

**Recovery position** exists for one reason: gravity. Putting an unresponsive but breathing patient on their side lets vomit and secretions drain out instead of down the trachea.

**Left lateral recumbent** is the specific position for a pregnant patient in the third trimester. The heavy uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when she lies flat, which cuts blood return to the heart and drops her pressure. Rolling her onto the left side takes the weight off that vein.

> **Trap:** Trendelenburg was taught for decades as the shock position. Current evidence does not support it, and it can worsen breathing by pushing abdominal contents against the diaphragm. Follow your protocol rather than the tradition.

## Movement terms

Flexion bends a joint and extension straightens it. Abduction moves a limb away from the midline and adduction brings it back, which is easy to remember because adduction adds the limb back to the body.

> **On shift:** The phrase you will write most often is some version of "distal pulses, motor and sensation intact in all four extremities." It means you checked circulation, movement and feeling past the injury, and it is the standard proof that a splint or immobilization did not cause harm.
keyPoints: Anatomical position is standing, facing forward, palms forward; left and right always belong to the patient.
Proximal is closer to the trunk and distal is farther; medial is toward midline and lateral is away.
Supine is face up, prone is face down, recovery position is on the side for airway drainage.
Fowler's is upright 60–90 degrees and semi-Fowler's is 30–45 degrees.
Third-trimester pregnant patients go left lateral recumbent to unload the inferior vena cava.

checks.q: Which statement is correct?
choices: The wrist is proximal to the elbow
The knee is distal to the hip
The thumb is medial to the pinky
The sternum is posterior to the spine
checks.why: Proximal and distal reference the attachment to the trunk, so the knee is farther out than the hip and is therefore distal to it. The wrist is distal to the elbow, the thumb is lateral, and the sternum is anterior.

checks.q: A 34-week pregnant patient becomes lightheaded and hypotensive lying flat. What position helps and why?
choices: Prone, to relieve pressure on the spine
Trendelenburg, to increase blood return by gravity
Left lateral recumbent, to take uterine weight off the inferior vena cava
checks.why: A third-trimester uterus compresses the vena cava when the patient is supine, cutting venous return and dropping pressure. Rolling her to the left relieves that compression directly; the other positions do not address the cause.

checks.q: An unresponsive adult is breathing adequately with a strong pulse and no suspected spinal injury. Which position protects the airway?
checks.why: The recovery position uses gravity to drain vomit and secretions out of the mouth rather than into the trachea. Supine risks aspiration, prone blocks the face and chest, and an unresponsive patient cannot be held sitting upright safely.

lessons.title: Planes, cavities, quadrants and regions
lessons.body:
## Planes: the three ways to slice the body

A plane is an imaginary flat cut, and imaging is described by which plane the picture was taken in.

| Plane | The cut | Divides the body into |
|---|---|---|
| Sagittal | vertical, front to back | left and right parts |
| Midsagittal (median) | vertical, exactly down the middle | equal left and right halves |
| Frontal (coronal) | vertical, side to side | front (anterior) and back (posterior) |
| Transverse (axial, cross-sectional) | horizontal | top (superior) and bottom (inferior) |

A `CT` scan produces transverse slices by default, which is why the images look like you are standing at the patient's feet looking up through them.

## Cavities: the spaces organs live in

The body has two main groups of cavities.

**Dorsal (posterior)**

- **Cranial cavity** — the brain
- **Spinal (vertebral) cavity** — the spinal cord

**Ventral (anterior)**

- **Thoracic cavity** — heart, lungs, great vessels, esophagus. It contains the mediastinum, the central compartment holding the heart.
- **Abdominal cavity** — stomach, intestines, liver, gallbladder, spleen, pancreas, kidneys
- **Pelvic cavity** — bladder, rectum, internal reproductive organs

The **diaphragm** separates thoracic from abdominal. Because it rises to about the level of the nipples on full exhalation, a stab wound to the lower chest can easily injure abdominal organs.

> **Key:** Anything between the nipple line and the umbilicus can be a chest injury, an abdominal injury, or both, because the diaphragm moves through that zone with every breath.

## The four quadrants

Draw two lines through the umbilicus, one vertical and one horizontal. That gives the four quadrants used in almost every abdominal complaint.

| Quadrant | Major contents |
|---|---|
| Right upper (`RUQ`) | Liver, gallbladder, right kidney, part of the colon |
| Left upper (`LUQ`) | Stomach, spleen, pancreas, left kidney |
| Right lower (`RLQ`) | Appendix, cecum, right ovary and tube |
| Left lower (`LLQ`) | Sigmoid colon, left ovary and tube |

That table does most of the clinical work. `RLQ` pain in a young adult means appendicitis until proven otherwise. `RUQ` pain after a fatty meal points at the gallbladder. `LUQ` tenderness after blunt trauma to the left ribs points at the spleen.

## The nine regions

A finer grid divides the abdomen into nine regions with two vertical and two horizontal lines.

| Row | Regions, left to right on the page |
|---|---|
| Upper | Right hypochondriac, epigastric, left hypochondriac |
| Middle | Right lumbar, umbilical, left lumbar |
| Lower | Right iliac (inguinal), hypogastric (suprapubic), left iliac |

Three of these names appear constantly. **Epigastric** pain is the classic description for both stomach problems and heart attacks, which is why epigastric pain gets an `ECG`. **Suprapubic** tenderness suggests the bladder. **Right iliac** is where appendicitis localizes, at a point known as McBurney's point.

> **Trap:** Pain location does not reliably name the organ. Gallbladder pain refers to the right shoulder, a heart attack refers to the jaw and left arm, and a ruptured spleen refers to the left shoulder, a finding called Kehr's sign.

> **On the exam:** Learn the quadrants cold and the nine regions by recognition. Vignettes are almost always written in quadrants, with epigastric and suprapubic used as the two exceptions.
keyPoints: Sagittal divides left and right, frontal divides front and back, transverse divides top and bottom.
Dorsal cavities hold brain and cord; ventral cavities are thoracic, abdominal and pelvic.
The diaphragm rises to about the nipple line, so lower chest wounds can injure abdominal organs.
Quadrants: RUQ liver and gallbladder, LUQ stomach and spleen, RLQ appendix, LLQ sigmoid colon.
Epigastric pain can be cardiac, and referred pain sends spleen injury to the left shoulder.

checks.q: A patient is kicked in the left lower ribs and develops left shoulder pain with no shoulder injury. What should you suspect?
checks.why: The spleen sits in the left upper quadrant under the lower ribs, and blood irritating the diaphragm refers pain to the left shoulder, known as Kehr's sign. The gallbladder is on the right and the appendix is in the right lower quadrant.

checks.q: Which plane divides the body into anterior and posterior portions?
checks.why: The frontal or coronal plane runs vertically side to side, separating front from back. Sagittal planes separate left from right and transverse planes separate top from bottom.

checks.q: A 58-year-old reports burning epigastric pain and nausea. What should be done early?
choices: Assume reflux and give an antacid only
Obtain an ECG, because epigastric pain can be cardiac
checks.why: Inferior heart attacks commonly present as epigastric burning with nausea rather than crushing chest pain, especially in older adults and people with diabetes. Treating it as reflux without an ECG is a well-documented way to miss an infarction.

lessons.title: The abbreviations you will actually hear
lessons.body:
## The shorthand is not optional

Charts, radio reports and shift handoffs run on abbreviations, and nobody will pause for you to look one up. Group them by where you meet them.

## Complaints and findings

| Short | Full | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `SOB` | shortness of breath | Also charted as dyspnea |
| `CP` | chest pain | |
| `AMS` | altered mental status | Always paired with a glucose check |
| `LOC` | level of consciousness, or loss of consciousness | Ambiguous, so write which you mean |
| `N/V/D` | nausea, vomiting, diarrhea | |
| `c/o` | complains of | |
| `s/p` | status post, meaning after | `s/p` fall |
| `LKW` | last known well | The clock that decides stroke treatment |
| `ROS` | review of systems | |
| `NKDA` | no known drug allergies | |
| `WNL` | within normal limits | |

## History, orders and plan

| Short | Full |
|---|---|
| `hx` | history |
| `PMH` | past medical history |
| `Dx` | diagnosis |
| `Tx` | treatment |
| `Rx` | prescription or therapy |
| `Sx` | symptoms |
| `PRN` | as needed, from Latin pro re nata |
| `STAT` | immediately, from Latin statim |
| `NPO` | nothing by mouth, from nil per os |
| `PTA` | prior to arrival |
| `DNR`, `POLST` | do not resuscitate, and the portable order form |

## Conditions you will hear hourly

| Short | Full |
|---|---|
| `MI` | myocardial infarction, a heart attack |
| `CVA` | cerebrovascular accident, a stroke |
| `TIA` | transient ischemic attack |
| `CHF` | congestive heart failure |
| `COPD` | chronic obstructive pulmonary disease |
| `DKA` | diabetic ketoacidosis |
| `PE` | pulmonary embolism |
| `UTI` | urinary tract infection |
| `DVT` | deep vein thrombosis |
| `ETOH` | alcohol |
| `GSW` | gunshot wound |
| `MVC` | motor vehicle collision |

## Arrival, place and route

`BIBA` is brought in by ambulance. `POV` is privately owned vehicle, meaning the patient drove or was driven. `ED` is the emergency department, `ICU` the intensive care unit, and `OR` the operating room.

Routes of medication:

| Route | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `PO` | by mouth |
| `IV` | intravenous |
| `IM` | intramuscular |
| `IN` | intranasal |
| `SL` | sublingual, under the tongue |
| `SQ`, `subQ` | subcutaneous |
| `IO` | intraosseous, into the bone |

Frequency and symbols: `q` means every, so `q4h` is every four hours. `BID` is twice daily, `TID` three times daily, `QID` four times daily. `×` means times, so `×2` is two doses. `Ø` means none. `a` with a bar over it means before and `p` with a bar means after. An arrow up or down is used for increased or decreased.

> **Trap:** `LOC` is the most dangerous abbreviation in routine use because it means two very different things. Loss of consciousness is an event that happened; level of consciousness is a measurement you took. Spell out which one you mean.

> **On shift:** A real handoff sounds like this. `BIBA` `62F` `c/o` `CP` `×2h`, `hx` `MI` and `COPD`, `s/p` aspirin `PTA`, `NKDA`, vitals `WNL` except `HR` `104`. Decoded: brought in by ambulance, a 62-year-old female complaining of chest pain for two hours, with a history of heart attack and chronic lung disease, who took aspirin before arrival, has no known drug allergies, and whose vital signs are normal except a heart rate of 104.
keyPoints: SOB shortness of breath, CP chest pain, AMS altered mental status, c/o complains of, s/p status post.
LKW last known well is the clock that decides stroke treatment eligibility.
PRN as needed, STAT immediately, NPO nothing by mouth, PTA prior to arrival.
Routes: PO mouth, IV vein, IM muscle, IN nasal, SL under tongue, SQ under skin, IO into bone.
LOC is ambiguous between loss of consciousness and level of consciousness, so spell it out.

checks.q: A chart reads: 71M BIBA, c/o SOB ×2d, hx COPD, s/p albuterol PTA, NKDA. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The patient walked in with two days of chest pain
A 71-year-old male arrived by ambulance with two days of shortness of breath and took albuterol before arrival
The patient has a known allergy to albuterol
The patient was given albuterol in the department
checks.why: BIBA is brought in by ambulance, SOB is shortness of breath, ×2d is for two days, s/p means after, PTA is prior to arrival, and NKDA means no known drug allergies. Nothing in the note says anything was given in the department.

checks.q: Why does LKW matter more than the time the ambulance was called in a suspected stroke?
choices: It determines which hospital the patient is billed to
It has no clinical use and is documented for records only
Last known well starts the clock that determines treatment eligibility
It identifies who witnessed the event for legal purposes
checks.why: Stroke therapies are time-limited from the moment the patient was last seen normal, not from when symptoms were noticed or help was called. A patient found down after waking has a last known well of bedtime, which can rule out treatment.

checks.q: An order reads: ondansetron 4 mg IV q6h PRN nausea. How is it given?
choices: 4 mg into the vein, no more than every 6 hours, only when nausea is present
4 mg by mouth every 6 hours around the clock
4 mg under the tongue immediately, one dose only
4 mg into the muscle, six times daily
checks.why: IV is intravenous, q6h is every six hours, and PRN means as needed rather than scheduled. PO would be by mouth, SL under the tongue, and IM into the muscle.

lessons.title: Dangerous abbreviations and the do-not-use list
lessons.body:
## Why a banned list exists

The Joint Commission publishes an official Do Not Use list, and every item earned its place by causing real harm. These are not style preferences. Each one has produced an overdose because a handwritten character was read as something else.

| Do not use | Read as | Write instead |
|---|---|---|
| `U` for unit | the number `0` or `4`, so `4U` becomes `40` | unit |
| `IU` for international unit | `IV`, or the number `10` | international unit |
| `Q.D.`, `QD`, `qd` | `QID`, four times daily, or the period read as an `I` | daily |
| `Q.O.D.`, `QOD` | `QD` or `QID` | every other day |
| Trailing zero, as in `1.0 mg` | `10 mg` when the decimal is missed | `1 mg` |
| Missing leading zero, as in `.5 mg` | `5 mg` | `0.5 mg` |
| `MS` | morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate | write the drug name |
| `MSO4`, `MgSO4` | each other | write the drug name |

## The decimal point rules, stated once

**Never write a trailing zero.** `1.0 mg` becomes `10 mg` the instant the decimal point is smudged, faxed poorly, or scanned. Write `1 mg`.

**Always write a leading zero.** `.5 mg` becomes `5 mg` the instant the decimal is missed. Write `0.5 mg`.

The asymmetry catches people out. One rule removes a zero, the other adds one, and both exist for exactly the same reason: a decimal point is the least reliable mark on a page.

> **Key:** A tenfold dosing error almost never comes from bad arithmetic. It comes from a decimal point nobody could see.

## Why the insulin ones are worst

`U` for unit is the most lethal item on the list because insulin and heparin are dosed in units and both are high-alert drugs. An order for `6U` of insulin read as `60` units is a hundredfold-scale error into a drug with a narrow margin.

The same logic makes `MS` dangerous. Morphine sulfate and magnesium sulfate are different drugs with different indications and very different consequences. Nothing about the abbreviation tells you which was meant.

## Others on the watch list

These are not on the official do-not-use list everywhere, but they appear on most institutional lists.

| Avoid | Problem | Write instead |
|---|---|---|
| `cc` | looks like `u`, meaning unit | `mL` |
| `µg` | mistaken for `mg`, a thousandfold error | `mcg` |
| `AD`, `AS`, `AU` | right ear, left ear, both ears, confused with the eye set | right ear, left ear, both ears |
| `OD`, `OS`, `OU` | right eye, left eye, both eyes | right eye, left eye, both eyes |
| `D/C` | discharge or discontinue, opposite meanings | write the word |
| `HS` | at bedtime, or half strength | at bedtime |
| `SC`, `SQ` | read as `SL` (sublingual) | subcutaneous |
| `TIW` | three times weekly, read as three times daily | three times weekly |

## What to do when you see one

If an order arrives with a banned abbreviation, you do not interpret it. You get it clarified by the prescriber and then documented in the safe form. Guessing correctly nine times does not offset the tenth.

> **Trap:** `D/C` is the one people defend because context usually makes it obvious. It does not always. `D/C` insulin at the bottom of a discharge summary can be read as stop the insulin or as it is on the discharge list, and those are opposite instructions.

> **On shift:** When you transcribe anything, write drug names in full, write `mL` and `mcg`, put a zero before every decimal and never after one, and spell out daily. Those five habits eliminate most of the list.
keyPoints: Write unit, not U; international unit, not IU; daily, not QD; every other day, not QOD.
Never write a trailing zero (1 mg, not 1.0 mg); always write a leading zero (0.5 mg, not .5 mg).
Never abbreviate morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate as MS, MSO4 or MgSO4.
Use mL not cc, and mcg not the Greek mu symbol, to avoid thousandfold errors.
A banned abbreviation in an order gets clarified with the prescriber, never interpreted.

checks.q: Which is written correctly?
checks.why: It carries a leading zero, no trailing zero, a full drug name and a spelled-out frequency. The others show a missing leading zero, the banned U for unit, and a trailing zero that can be read as 50 mg.

checks.q: Why is U the most dangerous abbreviation on the do-not-use list?
choices: It is hard to pronounce in a verbal order
It is used for a rarely prescribed class of drugs
It can be read as 0 or 4, and it is used for insulin and heparin, which are high-alert drugs
It has no accepted meaning in medicine
checks.why: A handwritten U next to a number reads as an extra digit, so 6U becomes 60, and the drugs dosed in units have very narrow safety margins. The abbreviation is well understood; that is exactly what makes it dangerous.

checks.q: A handwritten order reads: MS 4 mg IV q4h PRN pain. What is the correct action?
choices: Clarify with the prescriber, because MS could mean morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate
Give morphine, since MS almost always means morphine
Give magnesium, since it is the safer of the two
Document the order as written and proceed
checks.why: MS is banned precisely because it names two different drugs with different indications and different risks. Being right about the intended drug most of the time does not make interpreting it acceptable.

cards.front: What are the three parts a medical term can be built from?
cards.back: Root (the body part or core idea), prefix (modifies amount, speed, position or negation), suffix (says what is happening: condition, symptom or procedure).

cards.front: What is a combining vowel and when do you keep it?
cards.back: Usually an o, added for pronunciation only. Keep it before a consonant and between two roots; drop it before a vowel. Cardi + itis becomes carditis.

cards.front: What is the correct order for decoding a medical term?
cards.back: Backwards: suffix first, then prefix, then root. Pericarditis becomes inflammation, around, heart.

cards.front: Which two roots look alike but mean muscle versus spinal cord or marrow?
cards.back: My/o means muscle. Myel/o means spinal cord or bone marrow. Myalgia is muscle pain; myelopathy is spinal cord disease.

cards.front: Which roots mean heart, liver and nerve?
cards.back: Cardi/o heart, hepat/o liver, neur/o nerve. Examples: cardiomegaly, hepatitis, neuropathy.

cards.front: Why are there two roots for kidney and two for lung?
cards.back: One Greek, one Latin. Nephr/o and pulmon/o versus ren/o and pneumon/o. Greek roots build disease and procedure names, Latin roots build adjectives like renal artery.

cards.front: What are the roots for bone, skin and stomach?
cards.back: Oste/o bone, derm/o or dermat/o skin, gastr/o stomach. Osteomyelitis, dermatitis, gastrectomy.

cards.front: Which root is small intestine and which is large intestine?
cards.back: Enter/o is small intestine, col/o or colon/o is large intestine. Gastroenteritis affects stomach and small bowel; colitis affects the colon.

cards.front: What two meanings does pneum/o carry, and how do you tell?
cards.back: Lung and air. Context decides: pneumothorax is air in the chest, pneumonia is infection in lung tissue.

cards.front: Which roots mean vessel, vein and artery?
cards.back: Angi/o vessel (imaging and procedures), vas/o vessel (physiology), phleb/o vein, arteri/o artery. Angioplasty, vasoconstriction, phlebotomy, arteriosclerosis.

cards.front: What is the difference between cephal/o and encephal/o?
cards.back: Cephal/o is head, encephal/o is brain, literally in- plus head. Cephalalgia is headache; encephalitis is brain inflammation.

cards.front: Name the roots for nose, voice box, windpipe and airway branches.
cards.back: Rhin/o nose, laryng/o voice box, trache/o windpipe, bronch/o bronchi. Rhinorrhea, laryngospasm, tracheostomy, bronchodilator.

cards.front: What do cyst/o, lith/o and glyc/o mean?
cards.back: Cyst/o is bladder or fluid-filled sac, lith/o is stone, glyc/o is sugar. Cystitis, nephrolithiasis, hyperglycemia.

cards.front: Decode cholecystitis and cholelithiasis.
cards.back: Chol/e is bile. Cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder, the sac holding bile. Cholelithiasis is gallstones.

cards.front: Name five hem/o words and what each describes.
cards.back: Hemothorax is blood in the chest, hematoma is blood pooled in tissue, hematuria is blood in urine, hemoptysis is coughing blood, hematemesis is vomiting blood.

cards.front: Hyper- versus hypo-: meaning and a clinical example of each.
cards.back: Hyper- is above normal, as in hyperglycemia or hypertension. Hypo- is below normal, as in hypoglycemia or hypotension. Two letters apart, opposite treatments.

cards.front: Tachy- and brady-: what adult numbers define each for pulse and respirations?
cards.back: Tachycardia is over 100 beats per minute, bradycardia under 60. Tachypnea is over 20 breaths per minute, bradypnea under 12.

cards.front: What do a-/an-, dys- and eu- mean?
cards.back: A- or an- means without (apnea, no breathing). Dys- means difficult, painful or abnormal (dyspnea). Eu- means normal or good (eupnea).

cards.front: Define peri-, epi-, endo- and sub- with an example each.
cards.back: Peri- around (pericardium), epi- upon (epidermis), endo- within (endotracheal), sub- under (sublingual).

cards.front: Intra- versus inter-: what is the difference?
cards.back: Intra- means within, as in intramuscular, inside the muscle. Inter- means between, as in intercostal, between the ribs. One letter, different location.

cards.front: What do hemi-, bi-, uni-, quadri- and para- mean?
cards.back: Hemi- half, bi- two, uni- one, quadri- four, para- beside or two like parts. Hemiparesis, bilateral, unilateral, quadriplegia, paraplegia.

cards.front: Poly- versus oligo-, with a urine example of each.
cards.back: Poly- is many or much, as in polyuria, excessive urination. Oligo- is few or scanty, as in oliguria, scanty urine output.

cards.front: Dysphagia versus dysphasia?
cards.back: Phag/o is swallowing, so dysphagia is difficulty swallowing. Phas/o is speech, so dysphasia is difficulty speaking. Both appear in stroke presentations.

cards.front: What do -itis, -osis, -emia and -uria mean?
cards.back: -itis inflammation, -osis abnormal condition, -emia a blood condition, -uria a urine condition. Appendicitis, cyanosis, anemia, hematuria.

cards.front: What do -oma, -megaly and -pathy mean?
cards.back: -oma is a tumor or mass, -megaly is enlargement, -pathy is disease. Hematoma, cardiomegaly, neuropathy.

cards.front: -rrhage versus -rrhea?
cards.back: -rrhage or -rrhagia means bursting forth, heavy bleeding, as in hemorrhage. -rrhea means a flow or discharge, as in rhinorrhea or diarrhea.

cards.front: -plegia versus -paresis?
cards.back: -plegia is complete paralysis with no movement. -paresis is weakness with some movement preserved. Hemiplegia versus hemiparesis is a meaningful difference in a stroke.

cards.front: Distinguish -ectomy, -otomy and -ostomy.
cards.back: -ectomy is surgical removal (nephrectomy). -otomy is cutting into (thoracotomy). -ostomy is creating a permanent opening (colostomy, tracheostomy).

cards.front: What do -scopy, -gram and -graphy mean?
cards.back: -scopy is looking inside with an instrument (colonoscopy). -gram is the record or image produced (electrocardiogram). -graphy is the process of recording (angiography).

cards.front: What do -algia, -pnea and -emesis mean?
cards.back: -algia is pain (myalgia), -pnea is breathing (dyspnea, apnea), -emesis is vomiting (hematemesis, vomiting blood).

cards.front: What is anatomical position, and whose left is left?
cards.back: Standing upright, facing forward, arms at sides, palms forward. Left and right always belong to the patient, never the examiner.

cards.front: Proximal versus distal, with an example.
cards.back: Proximal is closer to the trunk, distal is farther from it. The elbow is proximal to the wrist; the wrist is distal to the elbow.

cards.front: Medial versus lateral?
cards.back: Medial is toward the midline, lateral is away from it. The thumb is lateral to the pinky in anatomical position.

cards.front: What do ventral and dorsal mean in humans?
cards.back: Ventral equals anterior (front), dorsal equals posterior (back). The top of the foot is the dorsum, where the dorsalis pedis pulse is felt.

cards.front: Supine versus prone?
cards.back: Supine is lying face up on the back, the default position for assessment and CPR. Prone is lying face down.

cards.front: What angles define Fowler's and semi-Fowler's?
cards.back: Fowler's is sitting upright at about 60 to 90 degrees, used for breathing difficulty. Semi-Fowler's is the head raised about 30 to 45 degrees.

cards.front: When and why is the recovery position used?
cards.back: For an unresponsive patient who is breathing with a pulse and no suspected spinal injury. Lying on the side lets vomit and secretions drain out instead of into the trachea.

cards.front: Why does a third-trimester pregnant patient go left lateral recumbent?
cards.back: Lying flat lets the uterus compress the inferior vena cava, cutting venous return and dropping blood pressure. Rolling left takes that weight off the vein.

cards.front: What is Trendelenburg position and what is its current status?
cards.back: Flat with the whole body tilted head-down and feet elevated. Long taught for shock, now rarely recommended because it can impair breathing. Follow protocol.

cards.front: Name the three body planes and what each divides.
cards.back: Sagittal divides left and right, frontal or coronal divides front and back, transverse or axial divides top and bottom.

cards.front: What are the dorsal and ventral body cavities?
cards.back: Dorsal: cranial (brain) and spinal (cord). Ventral: thoracic (heart, lungs, great vessels), abdominal (digestive organs, spleen, kidneys), pelvic (bladder, rectum, reproductive organs).

cards.front: Why can a lower chest wound injure abdominal organs?
cards.back: The diaphragm rises to about the nipple line on full exhalation, so the boundary between chest and abdomen moves with every breath.

cards.front: Name the major organs in each abdominal quadrant.
cards.back: RUQ liver and gallbladder. LUQ stomach, spleen and pancreas. RLQ appendix and cecum. LLQ sigmoid colon. Kidneys sit behind the upper quadrants.

cards.front: Which quadrant points to appendicitis, and what is that point called?
cards.back: Right lower quadrant. The localized tender spot is McBurney's point, about a third of the way from the hip bone to the umbilicus.

cards.front: Name the nine abdominal regions.
cards.back: Top row: right hypochondriac, epigastric, left hypochondriac. Middle: right lumbar, umbilical, left lumbar. Bottom: right iliac, hypogastric, left iliac.

cards.front: Why does epigastric pain get an ECG?
cards.back: Inferior heart attacks often present as epigastric burning with nausea instead of chest pain, especially in older adults and people with diabetes.

cards.front: What is Kehr's sign?
cards.back: Left shoulder pain from blood irritating the diaphragm after splenic injury. A referred pain pattern, so the painful spot is nowhere near the injured organ.

cards.front: Decode this handoff: BIBA 62F c/o CP ×2h, hx MI, s/p ASA PTA, NKDA.
cards.back: Brought in by ambulance, 62-year-old female complaining of chest pain for two hours, history of heart attack, took aspirin before arrival, no known drug allergies.

cards.front: What do PRN, STAT and NPO mean?
cards.back: PRN is as needed (pro re nata), STAT is immediately (statim), NPO is nothing by mouth (nil per os).

cards.front: What is LKW and why does it matter?
cards.back: Last known well, the time the patient was last seen normal. Stroke treatment windows run from that moment, not from when symptoms were noticed or 911 was called.

cards.front: Give the meanings of PO, IV, IM, IN, SL, SQ and IO.
cards.back: By mouth, intravenous, intramuscular, intranasal, sublingual (under the tongue), subcutaneous (under the skin), intraosseous (into the bone).

cards.front: What do q, BID, TID and QID mean?
cards.back: q means every, so q4h is every four hours. BID is twice daily, TID three times daily, QID four times daily.

cards.front: Why is LOC a dangerous abbreviation?
cards.back: It means both loss of consciousness, an event, and level of consciousness, a measurement. The two readings can lead to opposite conclusions, so spell out which you mean.

cards.front: Expand MI, CVA, CHF, COPD, DKA and PE.
cards.back: Myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular accident (stroke), congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetic ketoacidosis, pulmonary embolism.

cards.front: Expand ETOH, GSW, MVC, BIBA and POV.
cards.back: Alcohol, gunshot wound, motor vehicle collision, brought in by ambulance, privately owned vehicle.

cards.front: State the two decimal point rules and why each exists.
cards.back: Never a trailing zero: 1.0 mg reads as 10 mg. Always a leading zero: .5 mg reads as 5 mg. A decimal point is the least reliable mark on a page.

cards.front: Why are U and IU banned?
cards.back: U reads as 0 or 4, so 6U becomes 60, and IU reads as IV or 10. Both are used for insulin and heparin, high-alert drugs with narrow margins. Write unit and international unit.

cards.front: Why are MS, MSO4 and MgSO4 banned?
cards.back: MS means morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate, and MSO4 and MgSO4 are mistaken for each other. Different drugs, different indications. Write the full name.

cards.front: Why write daily instead of QD?
cards.back: QD is read as QID, four times daily, and a period in Q.D. can look like an I. Write daily, and write every other day instead of QOD.

cards.front: What do you do when an order arrives using a banned abbreviation?
cards.back: Clarify it with the prescriber and document the safe form. You do not interpret it, because being right nine times does not offset the tenth.

quiz.q: Which spelling correctly applies the combining vowel rule to gastr plus itis?
quiz.why: The suffix begins with a vowel, so the combining vowel is dropped and the word is gastritis. Keeping the o would be correct only before a consonant, as in gastroscopy.

quiz.q: A chart lists a diagnosis of endocarditis. What does that word describe?
choices: Inflammation of the sac around the heart
Disease of the heart valves without inflammation
Inflammation of the inner lining of the heart
quiz.why: Endo- means within, cardi is heart, and -itis is inflammation, so endocarditis is inflammation of the heart's inner lining and valves. Inflammation of the surrounding sac is pericarditis, and enlargement is cardiomegaly.

quiz.q: Which pair of roots refers to the same organ?
quiz.why: Nephr/o is Greek and ren/o is Latin, but both mean kidney and both appear in practice. My/o is muscle versus cord or marrow, hepat/o is liver versus blood, and enter/o is small bowel versus large bowel.

quiz.q: A trauma patient is diagnosed with a hemothorax rather than a pneumothorax. What is the difference?
choices: Hemothorax is on the left and pneumothorax is on the right
Hemothorax involves lung tissue infection; pneumothorax does not
Hemothorax is blood in the chest cavity; pneumothorax is air
They are two names for the same finding
quiz.why: Hem/o is blood and pneum/o here means air, and both sit in the thoracic cavity outside the lung. Infection in lung tissue is pneumonia, which is a different use of the same root.

quiz.q: What does the term gastroenteritis specifically involve?
choices: The stomach and the small intestine
The entire digestive tract including the mouth
quiz.why: Gastr/o is stomach and enter/o is small intestine, so the term names inflammation of both. The colon would require col/o, giving colitis, and the liver would require hepat/o.

quiz.q: A patient is coughing up blood. Which term belongs in the chart?
quiz.why: Hemoptysis is blood spit up from the airway, while hematemesis is blood vomited from the gastrointestinal tract. Hematuria is blood in urine and hemothorax is blood in the chest cavity, so all four name different sources.

quiz.q: What does the procedure name phlebotomy tell you about what was done?
choices: A vessel was imaged with contrast
A vein was permanently opened to the skin surface
A vein was cut into, as when drawing blood
quiz.why: Phleb/o is vein and -otomy is cutting into, which is exactly what a needle stick for a blood draw does. A permanent opening would be -ostomy, repair would be -plasty, and imaging would be -graphy.

quiz.q: Decode nephrolithiasis.
choices: The condition of having kidney stones
quiz.why: Nephr/o is kidney, lith is stone, and -iasis names a condition. Inflammation would be nephritis, removal would be nephrectomy, and pus in urine is pyuria.

quiz.q: An adult has a heart rate of 48 and a respiratory rate of 10. Which two terms apply?
quiz.why: Adult bradycardia is a pulse under 60 and bradypnea is a respiratory rate under 12, so both values are slow. Tachy- terms would require a pulse over 100 or a rate over 20.

quiz.q: A nitroglycerin tablet is placed under the tongue. Which term describes that route?
quiz.why: Sub- is under and lingu/o is tongue, so sublingual is under the tongue, where rich blood supply gives rapid absorption. Subcutaneous is under the skin, and the other two routes miss the site entirely.

quiz.q: A stroke patient has weakness affecting the right arm and right leg but can still move both slightly. Which term is most accurate?
quiz.why: Hemi- means one side of the body and -paresis means weakness with movement preserved, which fits exactly. Hemiplegia would require complete paralysis, paraplegia affects both legs, and quadriplegia affects all four limbs.

quiz.q: A patient reports painful urination. Which term belongs in the chart?
quiz.why: Dys- means painful or difficult and -uria is a urine condition, so dysuria is painful urination. Polyuria is excessive volume, oliguria is scanty output, and anuria is no urine at all.

quiz.q: A patient has a permanent surgical opening in the neck for breathing. Which suffix names that procedure and which term is correct?
quiz.why: -ostomy means creating a permanent opening, which is the stoma you can see. -otomy is a simple incision, -ectomy is removal, and -plasty is surgical repair.

quiz.q: Which term names a condition of the blood rather than an act of bleeding?
quiz.why: The suffix -emia denotes a blood condition, so hypoxemia is low oxygen in the blood. Hemorrhage and menorrhagia use -rrhage for bursting forth, and otorrhea is a discharge from the ear.

quiz.q: A physician performs a thoracentesis. What happened?
choices: The chest was imaged with contrast dye
A scope was passed into the airway
A needle punctured the chest to withdraw fluid
quiz.why: -centesis means puncture to withdraw fluid, so thoracentesis drains fluid from the chest. Surgical opening is thoracotomy, imaging with contrast uses -graphy, and passing a scope is bronchoscopy.

quiz.q: Which statement about proximal and distal is correct?
choices: The ankle is proximal to the knee
The shoulder is distal to the elbow
The fingers are distal to the wrist
Proximal and distal describe front and back
quiz.why: Distal means farther from the point of attachment to the trunk, and the fingers are farther out than the wrist. The ankle is distal to the knee, the shoulder is proximal to the elbow, and front and back are anterior and posterior.

quiz.q: A 36-week pregnant patient becomes pale and hypotensive while lying flat on a backboard. What is the best immediate action?
choices: Place her prone to reduce abdominal pressure
Tilt the board so she lies on her left side
Sit her fully upright in Fowler's position
Place her in Trendelenburg to boost venous return
quiz.why: Supine positioning lets the uterus compress the inferior vena cava, cutting venous return and dropping pressure, and tilting left relieves it immediately. Trendelenburg does not remove the uterine weight, and prone is not survivable for a term pregnancy.

quiz.q: An unresponsive adult with a pulse and adequate breathing vomits. No spinal injury is suspected. Which position is indicated?
choices: Supine with the head of the bed flat
Prone with the face turned down
quiz.why: Lying on the side lets gravity drain vomit out of the mouth rather than into the trachea, which is the entire purpose of the position. Supine and Trendelenburg both direct vomit toward the airway, and prone obstructs the face and chest.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old has migrating pain that settles in the right lower quadrant with tenderness at McBurney's point. Which organ is implicated?
quiz.why: The appendix sits in the right lower quadrant and localizes at McBurney's point as inflammation reaches the peritoneum. The gallbladder is right upper quadrant, and the spleen and stomach are both left upper quadrant.

quiz.q: A CT scan is described as showing transverse images. What does that mean about the slices?
choices: They divide the body into left and right
They divide the body into front and back
They follow the curve of the spine
They divide the body into superior and inferior portions
quiz.why: A transverse or axial plane cuts horizontally, separating what is above from what is below, which is why the images look like cross sections. Left and right is sagittal, and front and back is frontal or coronal.

quiz.q: A patient is stabbed just below the left nipple. Why must abdominal injury be considered?
choices: The diaphragm rises to about the nipple line on exhalation, so the wound can cross into the abdomen
The stomach normally sits inside the chest cavity
The pelvic cavity extends up to the ribs
quiz.why: The diaphragm moves several centimeters with every breath, so the boundary between thoracic and abdominal cavities is not fixed at the rib margin. A wound at the nipple line during exhalation can pass into the spleen, stomach or liver.

quiz.q: A radio report states: BIBA, 45M, c/o CP ×1h, s/p nitroglycerin PTA, NKDA. What happened before arrival?
choices: The patient was given nitroglycerin in the emergency department
The patient took nitroglycerin before arriving
The patient is allergic to nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin was refused by the patient
quiz.why: s/p means status post, meaning after, and PTA means prior to arrival, so the dose was taken before the patient reached the hospital. NKDA states there are no known drug allergies, which rules out the allergy option.

quiz.q: A patient with slurred speech woke at 06:00 with symptoms after going to bed well at 22:00. What is the last known well time?
choices: The time the ambulance was called
22:00, when the patient was last seen normal
The time of arrival at the emergency department
quiz.why: Last known well is the last moment the patient was verified to be at baseline, which here is bedtime, not waking. A wake-up stroke carries an LKW of the night before, which commonly places the patient outside standard treatment windows.

quiz.q: An order reads: acetaminophen 650 mg PO q6h PRN fever. How should it be administered?
choices: Into the vein every six hours around the clock
Under the tongue as a single immediate dose
Into the muscle six times each day
By mouth, no more often than every six hours, only if fever is present
quiz.why: PO is by mouth, q6h sets a minimum six-hour interval, and PRN means as needed rather than scheduled. The other options change the route or turn a conditional order into a standing one.

quiz.q: Which medication order is written in the safest form?
choices: Morphine MS 2.0 mg IV q4h PRN
quiz.why: It has a leading zero, no trailing zero, a full drug name and a spelled-out frequency. The others use the banned U for unit, omit a leading zero while using QD, and combine the banned MS abbreviation with a trailing zero.

quiz.q: Why is a trailing zero prohibited in dose writing?
choices: If the decimal point is missed, 1.0 mg is read as 10 mg
It makes the order longer than necessary
Trailing zeros are only used in pediatric dosing
It conflicts with metric unit conventions
quiz.why: A faint, smudged or poorly scanned decimal point turns the dose into a tenfold overdose, which is the only reason the rule exists. The leading zero rule exists for the mirror image problem, where .5 mg is read as 5 mg.

quiz.q: A handwritten order reads: insulin regular 8U subQ before meals. What is wrong and what is the risk?
choices: Nothing is wrong; U is an accepted abbreviation for unit
The route is wrong; insulin must be given intravenously
U can be read as 0, turning 8 units into 80 units of a high-alert drug
The timing is wrong; insulin is given only at bedtime
quiz.why: U written next to a number reads as an extra digit, and insulin is a high-alert drug where a tenfold error causes severe hypoglycemia. Subcutaneous is a correct route for regular insulin and before meals is a normal schedule, so the abbreviation is the sole defect.

quiz.q: A note reads: D/C metoprolol. Why is this unsafe?
choices: D/C is not used anywhere in medicine
D/C refers only to direct current
D/C can mean discharge or discontinue, which are opposite instructions
quiz.why: Read as discontinue it stops the drug; read as discharge it means the drug goes home with the patient, and the two produce opposite outcomes. Context usually clarifies it but not always, which is why the word should be written out.

scenarios.title: Classroom: decoding a radio report and a triage note
scenarios.intro:
No new medicine here. You are going to take a real-sounding radio report and a real-sounding triage note apart, one phrase at a time, until nothing in them is unfamiliar.

Work the same way every time: find the suffix, then the prefix, then the root. For abbreviations, ask whether you are reading a complaint, a history item, a treatment, or a time.

steps.prompt:
The radio crackles.

"Medic 4 to County, en route with a `58M`, `BIBA`, `c/o` `SOB` `×3` days, `hx` `COPD` and `CHF`, `NKDA`, `s/p` albuterol neb `PTA`. Vitals to follow."

What is the patient's complaint and what was already done?

choices.text: A 58-year-old male with three days of shortness of breath who received an albuterol treatment before arrival.
choices.feedback: Correct. `c/o` is complains of, `SOB` is shortness of breath, `×3` days is duration, `s/p` is status post meaning after, and `PTA` is prior to arrival. `NKDA` adds that there are no known drug allergies.

choices.text: A 58-year-old male with chest pain who is allergic to albuterol.
choices.feedback: Two errors worth naming. `SOB` is shortness of breath, not chest pain, which would be `CP`. And `NKDA` is the opposite of an allergy statement: no known drug allergies.

choices.text: A 58-year-old male with breathing trouble; the albuterol is an order for the receiving hospital to carry out.
choices.feedback: The complaint is right. But `s/p` plus `PTA` places the albuterol firmly in the past, before the patient reached anyone. Nothing in that report is an order.

steps.prompt:
The report continues: `hx` `COPD` and `CHF`.

Expand both, and say what each tells you about this patient's breathing problem.

choices.text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and congestive heart failure: one is a lung cause of breathlessness, the other a pump cause.
choices.feedback: Exactly, and that is why both matter here. `COPD` decodes as chronic, obstructive, pertaining to the lung (`pulmon/o`), disease. `CHF` is a failing pump backing blood into the lungs. Shortness of breath in this patient could come from either.

choices.text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and chronic heart fibrillation.
choices.feedback: The first is right. `CHF` is congestive heart failure, not fibrillation. Atrial fibrillation is charted as `AF` or `A-fib`, and it is a rhythm problem rather than a pump-strength problem.

choices.text: Both are lung diseases, so this is purely a respiratory problem.
choices.feedback: This is the reasoning error the terminology is supposed to prevent. `Pulmon/o` inside `COPD` is a lung root, but `CHF` contains no lung root at all. Reading the parts keeps you from collapsing two different organs into one.

steps.prompt:
In triage the note reads: `Pt` with dyspnea and orthopnea. `Hx` `CVA` two years ago with residual right hemiparesis. `C/o` bilateral lower extremity edema, worse `PM`.

What does right hemiparesis tell you, and what does bilateral lower extremity edema describe?

choices.text: Complete paralysis of the right side, and swelling in one leg.
choices.feedback: Both are close but wrong in ways that matter. `-Paresis` is weakness with movement preserved; complete paralysis would be `-plegia`. And `bilateral` means both sides, not one, which changes the differential entirely.

choices.text: Weakness, not paralysis, of the right side of the body, and swelling in both legs.
choices.feedback: Right. `Hemi-` is half or one side, `-paresis` is weakness with some movement, and `bi-` in `bilateral` is both. Swelling in both legs points at a systemic cause such as heart failure, while one swollen leg would raise clot concerns.

choices.text: Weakness of the right side, and swelling of the upper limbs.
choices.feedback: The hemiparesis is right. `Lower extremity` means the legs; the arms would be upper extremity. Getting the region wrong sends you looking at the wrong half of the patient.

steps.prompt:
The physician writes a working diagnosis you have never seen: **acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema, rule out pneumonitis.**

Decode `pneumonitis` using the method, without looking it up.

choices.text: Suffix `-itis` is inflammation and `pneumon/o` is lung, so inflammation of lung tissue.
choices.feedback: That is the method working. Decode from the back: `-itis` sets the category as inflammation, and `pneumon/o` names the organ. You do not need to have met the word before.

choices.text: It must mean air in the chest, because `pneum/o` means air.
choices.feedback: `Pneum/o` does carry both meanings, but the suffix decides. `-itis` is inflammation, which needs tissue to inflame, so the lung meaning is the one in play. Air in the chest would be `pneumothorax`, built from `thorac/o`.

choices.text: It means surgical removal of part of the lung.
choices.feedback: Removal is always `-ectomy`, as in `pneumonectomy`. Reading the suffix first would have caught this immediately, which is the whole reason the method runs backwards.

steps.prompt:
A handwritten order comes down with the chart: **furosemide 40 mg IV ×1, then insulin sliding scale, hold if glucose Ø, recheck QD. MgSO4 2 g IV if indicated.**

Two items in that order should stop you. Which ones?

choices.text: `QD` and `MgSO4`, both on the do-not-use list.
choices.feedback: Correct on both. `QD` is misread as `QID`, four times daily instead of once, and `MgSO4` is confused with `MSO4`, magnesium versus morphine. Write daily and write magnesium sulfate. The route abbreviations and `Ø` are not on the banned list.

choices.text: `IV` and `×1`, because symbols should never appear in orders.
choices.feedback: Both of those are standard and acceptable. `IV` is intravenous and `×1` is one dose. The banned list targets abbreviations that have actually caused dosing errors, not every piece of shorthand.

choices.text: `40 mg` and `2 g`, because doses should always be written in the same unit.
choices.feedback: Milligrams and grams are both correct units for their drugs and the mixture is normal. The defects here are abbreviations that get misread: `QD` and `MgSO4`.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern to keep: **read the suffix first, and never translate a root in isolation.**

Every unfamiliar term in this case gave itself up to the same three steps. `Pneumonitis` decoded without a dictionary because `-itis` set the category and forced the lung meaning of `pneumon/o` over the air meaning. `Hemiparesis` decoded precisely, and the precision mattered: weakness is not paralysis, and charting the wrong one overstates the deficit.

Abbreviations split into two piles. One pile is the working shorthand you must know cold, because reports move too fast to look anything up: `BIBA`, `c/o`, `s/p`, `PTA`, `hx`, `NKDA`, `SOB`, `CP`, `AMS`, `LKW`. The other pile is the banned list, where the correct response is never interpretation. `QD`, `U`, `IU`, `MS`, `MSO4`, `MgSO4`, a trailing zero and a missing leading zero all get clarified and rewritten.

Last thing: `bilateral` versus `unilateral` did real work in this case. Swelling in both legs suggests a systemic cause such as heart failure; swelling in one leg raises a clot. One prefix separated two very different patients.
